title: Kolbe before Auschwitz
hookLine: a friar with a printing press, a magazine for Mary, and a mission to Japan

cards: Ink on his fingers. A Polish Franciscan friar in round glasses bends over an old hand press, cranking out pages of a small magazine.
He has very little money and a weak chest, and his own brothers are not sure about this project. The magazine is called the Knight of the Immaculata. He hands copies out, mails them, begs for paper.

This path met Maximilian Kolbe at the end of his story, in a starvation cell, offering his life for another prisoner. Today goes back to the middle: the years when he was building something, loudly, with machines.

teach.b: First, the knight. As a young friar in Rome, Kolbe and a few companions started a movement they called the Militia Immaculatae, the army of the Immaculate, meaning Mary. A knight, in his sense, carried no sword.
He carried prayer and a promise to win people over to God through Mary, by any good means at hand. Second, the press. Back in Poland, his means at hand was paper.
He and his brothers built a friary near Warsaw, Niepokalanów, the city of the Immaculate, and filled it with presses and friars who ran them. Kolbe wanted the newest machines.
To him, a fast press was a tool for good, the same way a pulpit was. Third, Japan.

He sailed east and landed in Nagasaki with almost nothing, not even the language. Soon there was a Japanese edition of the magazine, and a small friary on a hillside outside the city. Fourth, the housetops.
Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light: and that which you hear in the ear, preach ye upon the housetops."
Kolbe treated the newest media of his day as a housetop.

The same knight who later stepped forward in Auschwitz spent his working years putting presses, paper and post to that use. Put as a question for today: can this carry something good to someone who needs it?

how: Catholics who join the Militia Immaculatae, the movement Kolbe started, consecrate themselves to Mary and pray for others, and Catholic media groups sometimes name Kolbe as an example for their work.

practice: Take out your phone, or just picture its screen, and notice what it usually carries: news, noise, arguments, photos, a few kind words.

Think of one person who could use something good today, a friend who's struggling, a parent who's lonely, and choose what you could send: a photo, a thank-you, a line that helped you. If you pray, offer that small message to God.
